content: Aerosinusitis, also referred to as barosinusitis, sinus squeeze, or sinus barotrauma, is a condition characterized by painful inflammation and, in some cases, bleeding of the mucosal lining of the paranasal sinus cavities, most commonly affecting the frontal sinus. This condition arises due to a disparity in air pressure between the inside and outside of the sinus cavities. It is frequently observed in scuba divers and aircraft pilots, and it is typically straightforward to diagnose when patients present to physicians immediately after exposure to pressure changes. However, diagnosis may be delayed or missed if the patient’s history does not clearly link symptoms to environmental pressure changes or if other potential causes are considered. Sinus barotrauma is often preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection or allergic reaction. Affected individuals experience a sudden, sharp facial pain or headache during descent, which intensifies as the aircraft approaches ground level. If the ambient pressure is not equalized, the pain can become debilitating. The pressure differential leads to swelling of the sinus mucosa, followed by submucosal bleeding, which further impairs sinus ventilation, particularly if the sinus openings (ostia) are involved. This process can result in the accumulation of fluid or blood within the sinus cavity. In most cases, sinus barotrauma manifests as localized pain in the frontal region. Less commonly, pain may radiate to the temporal, occipital, or retrobulbar areas. Epistaxis (nosebleeds) or serosanguineous nasal discharge may also occur. Neurological symptoms can arise if the adjacent fifth cranial nerve, particularly the infraorbital nerve, is affected. The condition has been recognized since the early days of aviation medicine, but it gained significant attention during World War II when its pathogenesis was linked to high-altitude flights. Rapid altitude changes and associated shifts in ambient pressure exposed aircrews to an increasing number of sinus barotrauma episodes. While fighter pilots experience the most extreme barometric stress, commercial aviation has also contributed to the disease’s prevalence. The underlying pathology of sinus barotrauma is governed by Boyle’s law, which states that the volume of a gas is inversely proportional to the pressure exerted on it, provided the temperature remains constant (P1 × V1 = P2 × V2). Two types of acute barotrauma are recognized: squeeze and reverse squeeze. During ascent, air within the paranasal sinuses expands, while it contracts during descent. Normally, the sinuses drain into the nasal cavity through small ostia, allowing for mucociliary clearance and pressure equalization. However, when these openings are obstructed by inflammation, polyps, mucosal thickening, anatomical abnormalities, or other lesions, pressure equalization becomes impossible. Squeeze occurs during descent when trapped air contracts, creating negative pressure within the sinuses. This pressure differential causes mucosal edema, transudation, and mucosal or submucosal hematoma, further occluding the sinus ostium. If the pressure differential is not neutralized, the sinus fills with fluid or blood. Conversely, reverse squeeze occurs during ascent if the sinus outlet is blocked, leading to increased pressure within the sinus, which can cause pain or epistaxis. Campbell and Weissman classified sinus barotrauma into three grades based on symptom severity. Grade I involves mild, transient sinus discomfort without radiographic changes. Grade II is characterized by severe pain lasting up to 24 hours, with some mucosal thickening visible on X-ray. Grade III presents with severe pain persisting for more than 24 hours, accompanied by significant mucosal thickening or opacification of the affected sinus on X-ray. Epistaxis or subsequent sinusitis may also be observed. The majority of sinus barotrauma cases involve the frontal sinuses, with pain localized to the frontal region. This may be attributed to the relatively long and delicate nasofrontal duct that connects the narrow frontal recess to the frontal sinuses. Barotrauma affecting the maxillary, ethmoidal, or sphenoidal sinuses is less common and typically occurs when the ostia are obstructed, often due to an acute upper respiratory tract infection. The pressure differential required to induce barotrauma likely varies significantly between individuals and depends on the size of the sinus ostium and the rate of ambient pressure change. Consequently, even commercial flights can result in severe barotrauma cases, although most occur in high-performance aircraft with lower pressurized cabins. Mild cases of barotrauma are effectively managed with topical decongestants and analgesics. In severe or treatment-resistant cases, functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) is indicated to restore sinus drainage and ventilation. This approach has demonstrated favorable outcomes in aviators with recurrent sinus barotrauma. Computer-aided surgery has been particularly effective in re-establishing drainage in affected sinuses, especially the sphenoid sinuses. Endoscopic examination of the sphenoid sinuses often reveals mucosal petechiae and hematomas.
